item.research_question: How does the addition of 0.71 wt.% Zr affect the microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of a CoCrFeMoNi high-entropy alloy designed for geothermal applications?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc remelting (VAR) using MRF ABJ 900 VAR equipment under argon atmosphere with six remelting operations for homogenization; samples ground and polished to mirror finish with 0.1 µm alumina suspension
item.test_conditions: Three-point bending test (ISO 7438:2020) for Young's modulus; microhardness test (1.96 N load, ISO 14577-1:2015); electrochemical tests in 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature including linear polarization (±25 mV vs Ecorr, 0.166 mV/s sweep), potentiodynamic polarization (-1.2 to +1.2 V vs SCE), and EIS (10⁻¹ to 10⁵ Hz)
key_findings: The Young's modulus of the Zr-free alloy (Sample 1) was 20.5% higher than that of the Zr-doped alloy (Sample 2).
The addition of Zr increased the average microhardness of the high-entropy alloy.
The corrosion rate increased from 2.44 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 1 to 2.80 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 2, representing a ~16-fold increase compared to Sample 1.
The polarization resistance (R2) of the passive film decreased from 2.57 × 10⁷ kΩ·cm² for Sample 1 to 1.47 × 10⁵ kΩ·cm² for Sample 2.
The addition of Zr caused grain refinement and reduced the volume fraction of interdendritic zones.
The tendency to form the sigma phase was diminished in Sample 2 due to a decrease in Mo concentration in interdendritic zones from 20 at.% to 17 at.%.
Both alloys exhibited brittle fracture with cleavage-like fracture planes.
item.mechanism: The decrease in corrosion resistance and passive film resistance with Zr addition is attributed to the formation of a thicker but more defective passive film containing an increased number of defective spots, potentially involving the in situ formation of ZrO2 which explains the high corrosion rate. The grain refinement and hardness increase are due to Zr obstructing grain coarsening and creating a supersaturated solid solution.
item.limitations: The volume fraction of ZrO2 was below the detection limit of XRD, preventing direct phase identification of the oxide despite TEM evidence in other studies.
quotes: The addition of Zr resulted in a decrease in the value of the Young modulus but also in a decrease in corrosion resistance.
The calculated CR data show values ranging from 2.44 × 10−3 mmpy for Sample 1 to 2.80 × 10−3 mmpy for Sample 2, representing a ~16-fold increase compared to Sample 1.
The formation of ZrO2 explained the high corrosion rate of Sample 2 with zirconium in comparison to Sample 1 without zirconium.

Question: How does the addition of 0.71 wt.% Zr affect the microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of a CoCrFeMoNi high-entropy alloy designed for geothermal applications?. System: CoCrFeMoNi (Sample 1) and CoCrFeMoNi + 0.71 wt.% Zr (Sample 2). Processing: Vacuum arc remelting (VAR) using MRF ABJ 900 VAR equipment under argon atmosphere with six remelting operations for homogenization; samples ground and polished to mirror finish with 0.1 µm alumina suspension. Test conditions: Three-point bending test (ISO 7438:2020) for Young's modulus; microhardness test (1.96 N load, ISO 14577-1:2015); electrochemical tests in 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature including linear polarization (±25 mV vs Ecorr, 0.166 mV/s sweep), potentiodynamic polarization (-1.2 to +1.2 V vs SCE), and EIS (10⁻¹ to 10⁵ Hz). Findings: The Young's modulus of the Zr-free alloy (Sample 1) was 20.5% higher than that of the Zr-doped alloy (Sample 2).; The addition of Zr increased the average microhardness of the high-entropy alloy.; The corrosion rate increased from 2.44 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 1 to 2.80 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 2, representing a ~16-fold increase compared to Sample 1.; The polarization resistance (R2) of the passive film decreased from 2.57 × 10⁷ kΩ·cm² for Sample 1 to 1.47 × 10⁵ kΩ·cm² for Sample 2.; The addition of Zr caused grain refinement and reduced the volume fraction of interdendritic zones.; The tendency to form the sigma phase was diminished in Sample 2 due to a decrease in Mo concentration in interdendritic zones from 20 at.% to 17 at.%.; Both alloys exhibited brittle fracture with cleavage-like fracture planes.. Mechanism: The decrease in corrosion resistance and passive film resistance with Zr addition is attributed to the formation of a thicker but more defective passive film containing an increased number of defective spots, potentially involving the in situ formation of ZrO2 which explains the high corrosion rate. The grain refinement and hardness increase are due to Zr obstructing grain coarsening and creating a supersaturated solid solution.. Limitations: The volume fraction of ZrO2 was below the detection limit of XRD, preventing direct phase identification of the oxide despite TEM evidence in other studies.. Quote: "The addition of Zr resulted in a decrease in the value of the Young modulus but also in a decrease in corrosion resistance."
